$$\operatorname{Var}(\ParameterSpaceDirection^T\PolicyGradientEstimate)
\le\left(\sum_{k=0}^{\TurnHorizon-1}\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(\ProjectedTurnGradientContribution_k)}\right)^2
\le \TurnHorizon^2\TurnContributionDeviationBound^2.$$

This is an upper bound under a uniform variance assumption, not a prediction of quadratic growth. If cross terms vanish, the bound becomes $\TurnHorizon\TurnContributionDeviationBound^2$. More generally, the additional assumption $\lvert\operatorname{Cov}(\ProjectedTurnGradientContribution_k,\ProjectedTurnGradientContribution_j)\rvert\le \TurnCovarianceBoundScale\TurnCovarianceDecayRatio^{\LaterRolloutTurnIndex-\RolloutTurnIndex}$ for constants $\TurnCovarianceBoundScale\ge0$ and $0\le\TurnCovarianceDecayRatio<1$ gives

$$\operatorname{Var}(\ParameterSpaceDirection^T\PolicyGradientEstimate)
\le \TurnHorizon\TurnContributionDeviationBound^2+2\TurnCovarianceBoundScale\sum_{\ell=1}^{\TurnHorizon-1}(\TurnHorizon-\ell)\TurnCovarianceDecayRatio^\ell
\le \TurnHorizon\left(\TurnContributionDeviationBound^2+\frac{2\TurnCovarianceBoundScale\TurnCovarianceDecayRatio}{1-\TurnCovarianceDecayRatio}\right).$$

A discount factor or a dense step reward does not establish that covariance assumption. Replacing a terminal criterion with learned process scores can also change the objective and introduce assessment error. The engineering comparison in @sec-vol3-rlvr-credit therefore asks what each estimator measures, how its uncertainty is assessed, and what obtaining its evidence costs. It does not infer sample efficiency from horizon or reward density alone.

### Conditional error bounds in trajectory imitation {#sec-vol3-appendix-math-compounding-error}

The bounds in @sec-vol3-fine-tuning-exposure-bias distinguish errors measured on reference-policy states from errors measured on learner-policy states. Neither bound predicts the realized cost of a particular agent. We derive the distinction for a finite horizon $\TurnHorizon$, a deterministic reference policy $\pi^*$, and a possibly stochastic learner $\pi$ with the same initial-state distribution and environment dynamics.

Let $\StateDistribution^t$ be the state distribution before decision $\TurnIndex$ under $\pi$, and $\StateDistribution=\TurnHorizon^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^\TurnHorizon \StateDistribution^t$. Include the relevant history in the state where needed. For immediate task cost $\ImmediateTaskCostScore(\PolicyObservedState,\PolicyAction)\in[0,1]$, define

$$\ExpectedTaskCostSum(\pi)=\sum_{t=1}^\TurnHorizon\mathbb E_{\PolicyObservedState\sim \StateDistribution^t,\;\PolicyAction\sim\pi(\cdot\mid \PolicyObservedState)}[\ImmediateTaskCostScore(\PolicyObservedState,\PolicyAction)].$$

Separately, let $\ReferenceDisagreementProbability(\PolicyObservedState,\pi)=\Pr_{\PolicyAction\sim\pi(\cdot\mid \PolicyObservedState)}[\PolicyAction\ne\pi^*(\PolicyObservedState)]$. This disagreement loss is not necessarily the task cost or the token-level training loss.

#### Errors on reference-policy states

Write $\ReferenceStepDisagreementRate_t=\mathbb E_{\PolicyObservedState\sim \ReferenceStateDistribution^t}[\ReferenceDisagreementProbability(\PolicyObservedState,\pi)]$ and $\ReferenceStateDisagreementRate=\TurnHorizon^{-1}\sum_t\ReferenceStepDisagreementRate_t$. Couple the two executions so they share environment randomness while their actions agree. Along a reference execution, draw hypothetical learner actions at each visited state. Until the first disagreement, these draws also describe the coupled learner.

By the union bound, the probability of at least one disagreement is at most $\sum_t\ReferenceStepDisagreementRate_t=\TurnHorizon\ReferenceStateDisagreementRate$. This argument needs no independence between disagreements. Before divergence, the coupled executions incur the same costs; afterward, their total cost difference is at most $\TurnHorizon$. Therefore

$$\ExpectedTaskCostSum(\pi)-\ExpectedTaskCostSum(\pi^*)\le \TurnHorizon\Pr(\text{any disagreement})
\le \min\{\TurnHorizon,\;\TurnHorizon^2\ReferenceStateDisagreementRate\}.$$

This yields the expert-distribution bound of @ross2011reduction, Theorem 2.1, with the additional trivial horizon cap. Marginal error bounds do not justify replacing the union bound by $1-(1-\ReferenceStepDisagreementRate)^\TurnHorizon$; that product requires further conditional-probability assumptions.

#### Errors on learner-policy states

Now let $\LearnerStateDisagreementRate=\mathbb E_{\PolicyObservedState\sim \StateDistribution}[\ReferenceDisagreementProbability(\PolicyObservedState,\pi)]$. Define $\ReferenceCostToGo(\PolicyObservedState,\PolicyAction)$ as expected cost from step $\TurnIndex$ through $\TurnHorizon$ after taking $\PolicyAction$ and then following $\pi^*$. Let

$$\ReferenceActionDisadvantage(\PolicyObservedState,\PolicyAction)=\ReferenceCostToGo(\PolicyObservedState,\PolicyAction)-\ReferenceCostToGo(\PolicyObservedState,\pi^*(\PolicyObservedState)).$$

Compare policies that switch from the learner to the reference after successively later steps. Their cost differences telescope, giving

$$\ExpectedTaskCostSum(\pi)-\ExpectedTaskCostSum(\pi^*)=
\sum_{t=1}^\TurnHorizon\mathbb E_{\PolicyObservedState\sim \StateDistribution^t,\;\PolicyAction\sim\pi(\cdot\mid \PolicyObservedState)}
[\ReferenceActionDisadvantage(\PolicyObservedState,\PolicyAction)].$$

Suppose $\ReferenceActionDisadvantage(\PolicyObservedState,\PolicyAction)\le \DeviationDisadvantage$ for every learner-reachable state and action, with $\DeviationDisadvantage\ge0$. The disadvantage is zero when the action agrees with the reference, so each expectation is at most $\DeviationDisadvantage$ times the corresponding disagreement probability. Thus

$$\ExpectedTaskCostSum(\pi)-\ExpectedTaskCostSum(\pi^*)\le\min\{\TurnHorizon,\;\DeviationDisadvantage \TurnHorizon\LearnerStateDisagreementRate\},$$

as in Theorem 2.2. Linear dependence on $\TurnHorizon$ requires a horizon-independent $\DeviationDisadvantage$; in general, $\DeviationDisadvantage$ can grow with the remaining horizon. If the immediate cost itself is disagreement, the simpler identity $\ExpectedTaskCostSum(\pi)=\TurnHorizon\LearnerStateDisagreementRate$ follows directly, but does not describe arbitrary task costs.

DAgger obtains reference labels at states visited during successive policy collections and aggregates the examples for supervised learning. Its guarantees also require the stated learning and sampling assumptions. Collecting such records alone neither proves a small population error for the released policy nor makes the distribution penalty vanish. The chapter uses these bounds to motivate coverage and evaluation, not to promise that a particular training method eliminates compounding errors.

## Coordination Models {#sec-vol3-appendix-math-coordination-models}

More workers can shorten a task, and more reviewers can change an error probability. Both conclusions depend on the overhead and dependence models, not on agent count alone.

### Multi-agent Amdahl's Law stationary root analysis {#sec-vol3-appendix-math-amdahl}

@Sec-vol3-multiagent-need models the speedup of splitting work across $\WorkerCount$ workers with a serial fraction and a coordination term (@eq-vol3-multiagent-speedup). To examine one possible scaling curve, suppose the normalized overhead is $\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)=\CoherencyCoefficient(\WorkerCount-1)+\PairwiseCoordinationCoefficient \WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)$. This assumption gives

$$\text{Speedup}(\WorkerCount) = \frac{1}{\NormalizedElapsedTimeRatio(\WorkerCount)}, \qquad \NormalizedElapsedTimeRatio(\WorkerCount) = (1 - \ParallelFraction) + \frac{\ParallelFraction}{\WorkerCount} + \CoherencyCoefficient (\WorkerCount - 1) + \PairwiseCoordinationCoefficient \WorkerCount (\WorkerCount - 1)$$

where $\ParallelFraction \in (0, 1]$ is the fraction of the fixed work that divides across workers. The nonnegative coefficients $\CoherencyCoefficient$ and $\PairwiseCoordinationCoefficient$, with $\CoherencyCoefficient+\PairwiseCoordinationCoefficient>0$, parameterize the assumed overhead. With $\PairwiseCoordinationCoefficient=0$ and $\ParallelFraction=1-\ContentionCoefficient$, $1/\NormalizedElapsedTimeRatio$ is the universal scalability law of @eq-vol3-multiagent-usl, so $\CoherencyCoefficient$ is its coherency coefficient. The term in $\PairwiseCoordinationCoefficient$ adds overhead that grows with the number of worker pairs. Their values are workload parameters, not universal properties of delegation. The physical domain is integer $\WorkerCount\ge 1$; on this domain $\NormalizedElapsedTimeRatio(\WorkerCount)>0$ and $\NormalizedElapsedTimeRatio(1)=1$. The following continuous relaxation identifies candidate worker counts to test.

Maximizing speedup on the physical domain means minimizing $\NormalizedElapsedTimeRatio(\WorkerCount)$. Extending the denominator to positive real $\WorkerCount$ for differentiation gives

$$\frac{d \NormalizedElapsedTimeRatio}{d \WorkerCount} = -\frac{\ParallelFraction}{\WorkerCount^2} + \CoherencyCoefficient + \PairwiseCoordinationCoefficient (2\WorkerCount - 1)$$

and setting the derivative to zero gives the stationary condition

$$\StationaryConditionPolynomial(\WorkerCount) = 2\PairwiseCoordinationCoefficient \WorkerCount^3 + (\CoherencyCoefficient - \PairwiseCoordinationCoefficient) \WorkerCount^2 - \ParallelFraction = 0$$

1. **Exactly one positive root.** The coefficients of $\StationaryConditionPolynomial(\WorkerCount)$, in order, are $2\PairwiseCoordinationCoefficient$, $\CoherencyCoefficient - \PairwiseCoordinationCoefficient$, $0$, and $-\ParallelFraction$. Whether $\CoherencyCoefficient - \PairwiseCoordinationCoefficient$ is positive or negative, the sequence of nonzero signs changes exactly once, so by Descartes' rule of signs $\StationaryConditionPolynomial$ has exactly one positive real root $\WorkerCount^*$. When $\PairwiseCoordinationCoefficient = 0$ the condition reduces to $\CoherencyCoefficient \WorkerCount^2 = \ParallelFraction$, so $\WorkerCount^* = \sqrt{\ParallelFraction / \CoherencyCoefficient}$, which with $\ParallelFraction=1-\ContentionCoefficient$ is the peak of @eq-vol3-multiagent-usl-peak.
2. **The denominator is strictly convex.** The second derivative,
   $$\frac{\DerivativeOperator^2 \NormalizedElapsedTimeRatio}{d \WorkerCount^2} = \frac{2\ParallelFraction}{\WorkerCount^3} + 2\PairwiseCoordinationCoefficient,$$
   is positive for every $\WorkerCount > 0$, so $\WorkerCount^*$ uniquely minimizes the extended denominator. If $\WorkerCount^*<1$, the constrained minimum is at $\WorkerCount=1$. Otherwise, evaluate the adjacent integers around $\WorkerCount^*$, subject to available capacity. Maximizing the reciprocal outside the physical domain is unnecessary and need not be valid.

Under this assumed overhead, speedup eventually falls as concurrency grows. A split shortens modeled elapsed time only if $\NormalizedElapsedTimeRatio(\WorkerCount)<1$ at some feasible integer $\WorkerCount>1$; that condition says nothing by itself about acceptance or cost. Fit any proposed overhead model to workload measurements, examine variation and fit error, and test its predictions at the contemplated worker counts. A stationary point is a scheduling hypothesis, not a deployment recommendation. @Sec-vol3-multiagent-evaluation makes the latter decision against the task's objective and constraints.

### Correlated failures in multi-agent quorum voting {#sec-vol3-appendix-math-correlated-quorum}

The voting example in @sec-vol3-multiagent-consensus concerns false approval of a candidate known to violate the assessed criterion. Agreement among reviewers is not the same problem as a distributed protocol choosing one value. To model the former, let $\ReviewerFalseApprovalIndicator_j=1$ indicate false approval by reviewer $\ReviewerIndex$, with an odd number $\WorkerCount$ of reviewers. If these indicators are independent Bernoulli variables with common probability $\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability$, the majority false-approval probability is

$$\Pr\left(\sum_{j=1}^{\WorkerCount}\ReviewerFalseApprovalIndicator_j>\frac{\WorkerCount}{2}\right)
=\sum_{k=(\WorkerCount+1)/2}^{\WorkerCount}\binom{\WorkerCount}{\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount}\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability^\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount(1-\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability)^{\WorkerCount-\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount}.$$

For $\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability<1/2$, this probability tends to zero as odd $\WorkerCount$ increases. That conclusion depends on the stated joint model; knowing each reviewer's marginal error rate is not enough.

A latent task propensity gives a different joint model. Let $\FalseApprovalPropensity$ denote the false-approval probability for a randomly selected candidate in the declared cohort, and assume $\ReviewerFalseApprovalIndicator_j\mid \FalseApprovalPropensity$ are independent Bernoulli variables with parameter $\FalseApprovalPropensity$. Conditional independence can describe separate samples at a fixed input even when the reviewers use identical weights. Across candidates with different propensities, however,

$$\mathbb{E}[\ReviewerFalseApprovalIndicator_j]=\mathbb{E}[\FalseApprovalPropensity]=\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability,\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(\ReviewerFalseApprovalIndicator_i,\ReviewerFalseApprovalIndicator_j)=\operatorname{Var}(\FalseApprovalPropensity)\quad (\PeerReviewerIndex\ne \ReviewerIndex).$$

The covariance follows from conditional independence and the law of total covariance. Since each marginal indicator is Bernoulli with probability $\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability$, its variance is $\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability(1-\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability)$. For $0<\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability<1$, the pairwise correlation is therefore

$$\CorrelationCoefficient=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\FalseApprovalPropensity)}{\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability(1-\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability)}.$$

This dependence arises from shared candidate difficulty in the model, not from an assertion that identical weights force dependent random draws at every fixed input. Communication between reviewers or other shared randomness would require an additional dependence model.

For the chapter's illustrative beta mixture, assume $\FalseApprovalPropensity\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\PropensityPriorApprovalShape,\PropensityPriorRejectionShape)$ with $\PropensityPriorApprovalShape,\PropensityPriorRejectionShape>0$. Its mean and variance give

$$\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability=\frac{\PropensityPriorApprovalShape}{\PropensityPriorApprovalShape+\PropensityPriorRejectionShape},\qquad
\CorrelationCoefficient=\frac{1}{\PropensityPriorApprovalShape+\PropensityPriorRejectionShape+1},\qquad
\PropensityPriorApprovalShape=\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability\left(\frac{1}{\CorrelationCoefficient}-1\right),\qquad
\PropensityPriorRejectionShape=(1-\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability)\left(\frac{1}{\CorrelationCoefficient}-1\right).$$

The parameterization applies for $0<\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability<1$ and $0<\CorrelationCoefficient<1$. Independence is the limiting constant-propensity case, not a beta distribution with finite shape parameters and $\CorrelationCoefficient=0$. Define the beta function locally by

$$\mathrm{B}(\PropensityPriorApprovalShape,\PropensityPriorRejectionShape)=\int_0^1 \FalseApprovalPropensityLevel^{\PropensityPriorApprovalShape-1}(1-\FalseApprovalPropensityLevel)^{\PropensityPriorRejectionShape-1}\,d\FalseApprovalPropensityLevel.$$

Integrating the conditional binomial probability over $\FalseApprovalPropensity$ gives the beta-binomial distribution for the false-approval count $\FalseApprovalCount=\sum_j\ReviewerFalseApprovalIndicator_j$:

$$\Pr(\FalseApprovalCount=\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount)=
\int_0^1 \binom{\WorkerCount}{\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount}\FalseApprovalPropensityLevel^\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount(1-\FalseApprovalPropensityLevel)^{\WorkerCount-\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount}
\frac{\FalseApprovalPropensityLevel^{\PropensityPriorApprovalShape-1}(1-\FalseApprovalPropensityLevel)^{\PropensityPriorRejectionShape-1}}{\mathrm{B}(\PropensityPriorApprovalShape,\PropensityPriorRejectionShape)}\,d\FalseApprovalPropensityLevel
=\binom{\WorkerCount}{\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount}\frac{\mathrm{B}(\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount+\PropensityPriorApprovalShape,\WorkerCount-\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount+\PropensityPriorRejectionShape)}{\mathrm{B}(\PropensityPriorApprovalShape,\PropensityPriorRejectionShape)}.$$

Summing over $\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount>\WorkerCount/2$ yields the majority false-approval probability; the $\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount=\WorkerCount$ term gives unanimous false approval. These are consequences of the full mixture assumption. Other joint distributions can share the same $\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability$ and $\CorrelationCoefficient$ while producing different majority probabilities.

The asymptotic result also has a precise scope. Conditional on $\FalseApprovalPropensity=\FalseApprovalPropensityLevel\ne1/2$, the sample fraction converges to $\FalseApprovalPropensityLevel$. The beta distribution has no point mass at $1/2$, so bounded convergence gives

$$\lim_{\substack{\WorkerCount\to\infty\\\WorkerCount\ \text{odd}}}
\Pr(\FalseApprovalCount>\WorkerCount/2)=\Pr(\FalseApprovalPropensity>1/2)
=\frac{1}{\mathrm{B}(\PropensityPriorApprovalShape,\PropensityPriorRejectionShape)}
\int_{1/2}^{1}\FalseApprovalPropensityLevel^{\PropensityPriorApprovalShape-1}(1-\FalseApprovalPropensityLevel)^{\PropensityPriorRejectionShape-1}\,d\FalseApprovalPropensityLevel.$$

In this model, adding reviewers cannot remove the cohort's mass of candidates that most reviewers tend to approve incorrectly. The result is not a universal error floor for all model ensembles. Measure the actual review policy on the intended cohort, retain evidence about its errors, and keep runtime authorization and scoped acceptance checks distinct from the vote.
